capabilities.target: Supabase database tables via service role (bypasses row level security), including support ticket tables and the integration_tokens table in the same database
support_messages table, rows rendered back to the customer in their own ticket thread

inputs.source: Developer prompt typed in the IDE ('Show me the latest open support tickets.')
Customer-written ticket message submitted through the public, unauthenticated support widget

elements.name: integration_tokens table, in the same database, reachable via the service-role credential
support_messages table, rows rendered back to the customer

controls.name: Per-tool-call developer approval prompt showing the SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced in the IDE client outside the model, and the developer sees the raw SQL text (raw_action), so it is not defeated by model capability alone. It does decay with approval volume: developers approving many calls per session are prone to approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403), rubber-stamping an insert that carries exfiltrated data, and a more capable model can phrase the request to look more routine.

controls.name: Least-privilege database role for the agent, with row level security enforced
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that cannot read integration_tokens and that respects row level security would make the sensitive read structurally unreachable regardless of model behavior or injected instructions.

controls.name: Pin or hash the Supabase MCP server package and tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the server version and hashing tool definitions prevents silent tool redefinition (rug pull) regardless of model capability.

controls.name: Secret/token scanner on writes to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: A separate classifier over outgoing content is enforced outside the primary model, but encoding or paraphrase can get past it, and it does not scale with the attacking model's capability.

controls.name: Action logging bound to the approving developer's identity
controls.decay_rationale: Logging does not prevent anything but creates an audit trail if reviewed, including which developer approved a query touching integration_tokens.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): ticket injection drives service-role read of integration_tokens, then a customer-visible insert exfiltrates them

attack_path.note: A customer embeds hidden instructions in a ticket message submitted through the public, unauthenticated support widget.
Responding to the developer's request to show open tickets, the agent runs SQL that reads ticket rows; the embedded instructions enter the agent's context.
The injected instructions direct the agent to query the integration_tokens table in the same database, which the service-role credential can read regardless of row level security.
The agent inserts the harvested token data into support_messages.
support_messages rows are rendered back to the same customer's ticket thread, completing exfiltration across the trust boundary.

forecast.watch_signal: Rising per-session tool-call approval counts with shrinking median review time per call; any IDE/client setting that enables batch or auto-approve; a model or version upgrade in the coding agent extension.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database -- the agent's credential is not scoped to the support ticket tables.

Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget with no stated authentication, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, creating a customer-visible egress channel fed by agent-authored content.

The IDE client asks for approval before each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, which is the approval-fatigue pattern a stronger or more persuasive model can exploit.
The MCP server config grants the agent an execute_sql capability backed by a long-lived access token, with no narrower scope than the service role described in the runtime notes.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role credential with a least-privilege role scoped to the support ticket tables, with row level security enforced, so the agent cannot read integration_tokens regardless of injected instructions.
Add a secret/token scanner on writes to customer-visible tables to block credentials or tokens from being echoed back to a customer.
Log and bind every execute_sql call to the approving developer's identity, and alert on any query touching integration_tokens or other credential tables.
Spotlight customer-authored ticket content as untrusted data in the agent's context so instructions embedded in it are not treated as directives.
Monitor and cap approvals per developer per session; require a second reviewer or a cooling-off step once volume crosses a threshold, to counter approval fatigue.

findings.title: ASI04: unpinned Supabase MCP server (@latest) permits undetected tool redefinition (rug pull)

attack_path.note: The server package is fetched fresh via 'npx -y ...@latest' on every invocation, with no version pin, hash, or peer identity verification, so a compromised or republished package can silently change behavior after the developer has already granted it trust.
A rug-pulled server can alter what execute_sql does server-side while still presenting an innocuous-looking SQL string to the per-call approval prompt.
The same compromised server can redirect or duplicate write results independent of the arguments the developer actually sees and approves.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: The npm package version or the tools/list schema for @supabase/mcp-server-supabase changes between sessions.

evidence.observation: mcpServers.supabase.args includes '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', which re-resolves to whatever version is currently published, with no pinning, hashing, or peer identity verification declared anywhere in the artifacts.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific, reviewed version and verify its package hash before use instead of using @latest.
Diff the tools/list response against a known-good baseline at session start and alert on any change to tool names, descriptions, or schemas.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an unauthenticated customer (U source) can write content that reaches a service-role SQL read of a restricted credentials table and then a customer-visible write (S3 sink), the classic lethal trifecta. The only present control on that path, a per-call developer approval prompt, is structural and shows raw SQL, which credits a two-tier reduction to moderate for finding f1 -- but the design separately runs an unpinned ('@latest'), unverified MCP server with no definition pinning, which is itself rated critical residual because nothing in the design covers that supply-chain exposure, so the overall residual rounds up to critical. The forecast is critical for both reasons: approval fatigue (developers approve many calls per session) is the specific control-decay path that defeats the approval gate on f1 under autonomy_increase, longer_task_horizon, or model_upgrade, which is exactly the failure mode behind the public incident this case backtests; and the unpinned server in f2 already has no mitigating control today, so a rug pull needs no additional trigger to reach the same sinks. The single highest-leverage structural fix is scoping the database credential away from the service role (ctl.scoped_db_credential), which would sever f1 entirely; the second is pinning the MCP server definition, which would close f2.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No system prompt or full tool manifest was provided; the complete set of tools exposed by the Supabase MCP server beyond execute_sql is unknown, so capability scope is inferred from the runtime notes at medium confidence.
The actual current contents of the '@latest' npm package were not inspected; the supply-chain finding is based solely on the absence of version pinning or hashing in the configuration.

Approval fatigue is inferred qualitatively from the statement that 'developers approve many calls in a session'; no quantitative approval rate or interface detail (for example, whether long queries are truncated in the prompt) was provided.
